source: World Religions II — lecture and readings, 2026-09-24

cards.front: Which region does World Religions II focus on?
cards.back: East Asia — the “global East”

cards.front: Which countries does the “global East” cover in this course?
cards.back: China, Japan, North and South Korea, and a little Vietnam

cards.front: Besides the countries themselves, who else is included in the course's scope?
cards.back: Diaspora communities

cards.front: How is the word “cult” used in this class?
cards.back: As a neutral term for a small religious group

cards.front: What does the neutral use of “cult” not rule out discussing?
cards.back: Religions considered dangerous, marginalised, or exploitative

cards.text: The instructor's criteria for religion (1–4): {{c1::a god, gods, or God}}; {{c2::a place of worship}}; {{c3::a holy book or scripture}}; {{c4::a leader, leaders, or specialists}}
The instructor's criteria for religion (5–8): {{c1::a founder}}; {{c2::actions}}; {{c3::belief}}; {{c4::faith}}
The instructor's criteria for religion (9–11): {{c1::vows}}; {{c2::exclusivity}}; {{c3::institutional acceptance — do other people think it is a religion?}}

cards.front: What does “institutional acceptance” mean as a criterion for religion?
cards.back: Whether other people regard it as a religion

cards.front: What did the class discussion offer as features of religion?
cards.back: Transmission, a theology or worldview, ritual devotional practice, sacred space, a historical figure, doctrine, faith, a higher power, and community

cards.front: How does the status of Siddhartha Gautama complicate a god-centred definition of religion?
cards.back: He is always a person who performs miracles, but not always a god

cards.front: How do East Asian traditions treat the line between supernatural and natural?
cards.back: As a continuum, rather than the clear line drawn in western religions

cards.front: Which two traditions are named as not focusing on the worship of a deity?
cards.back: Daoism and Confucianism

cards.front: What do some forms of Buddhism not require?
cards.back: Prayer or attendance at a temple — and some follow no sacred text

cards.front: Exclusivity is one of the instructor's criteria for religion — how do most East Asian religions stand on it?
cards.back: They fail it — most are inclusive rather than exclusive

cards.front: Which East Asian practice looks contradictory from a western definition of religion?
cards.back: Temples and praying directed at someone who is not a god

cards.front: What does the lecture say about people's views of a religion, including their own?
cards.back: They are often subjective

cards.front: What is said to be mutable about a religion?
cards.back: Which aspects are considered most important

cards.front: On what does the perceived importance of a religion's aspects depend?
cards.back: Place, time, and sect

cards.front: Which two countries in the region are officially atheist?
cards.back: China and North Korea

cards.front: What is the status of religion in North Korea officially?
cards.back: All religions are banned

cards.front: How many religions are permitted in China, and which?
cards.back: Five — Buddhism, Taoism, Islam, Protestantism, and Catholicism

cards.front: Despite official atheism, what is true in both China and North Korea?
cards.back: Things we could call religion are still practised

cards.text: Why praying or visiting a shrine may not count as religious practice: {{c1::practice and faith are only loosely associated}}; {{c2::some take a “try anything” approach}}; {{c3::religion can be a vessel for values or tradition rather than belief}}

cards.front: What stance does the course take on defining religion?
cards.back: To be flexible about what a religion is and how it is practised

cards.front: Which distinction does the lecture say to keep in mind throughout?
cards.back: Between doctrine or doxa — the texts — and how religion is practised or perceived

cards.text: The definitional problem runs both ways: {{c1::some things we would call a religion, its people do not}}; and {{c2::things we would not call religious, others do}}

cards.front: What kind of concept is the “Global East”, on the reading's account?
cards.back: A cultural and social one

cards.front: What does the Global East comprise?
cards.back: East Asian societies and ethnic communities, together with the diaspora

cards.front: Why does the reading argue the term “Global East” is needed?
cards.back: A Euro- or North-Atlantic-centric viewpoint cannot properly understand these communities

cards.front: When was the East/West division of the world most used, and why?
cards.back: During the Cold War, with its political and ideological battles

cards.front: Which division of the world became more popular from the 1970s, and what is it chiefly about?
cards.back: North versus South — chiefly developed versus others

cards.text: The reading's argument: the Global East fits {{c1::neither East/West nor North/South}}, because ideologically {{c2::some sided with the west and some with the east}} and economically {{c3::some count as global south despite lying in the northern hemisphere}}

cards.front: In which three Asian countries has communism persisted?
cards.back: China, North Korea, and Vietnam

cards.front: How does the reading say the persistence of communism should be treated?
cards.back: As having a large social impact that must be understood, not brushed off

cards.front: Which was the first developed country in East Asia, and which is named as currently surging?
cards.back: Japan was first; Vietnam is experiencing an economic upsurge

cards.front: What counter-example does the reading give to the global-north category?
cards.back: Some eastern European countries that were supposed to be global north are now struggling

cards.front: Who first argued for a link between religion and economy, and what link?
cards.back: Max Weber — between Protestantism and modern capitalism

cards.front: What is the reading's verdict on Max Weber?
cards.back: That many of his ideas are valuable but a lot of his main conceptualisations miss the mark

cards.front: What population comparison does the reading use against Euro-centric models?
cards.back: The western powers total about 1.1 billion, against about 2.3 billion in East and Southeast Asia — roughly 30% of the world the model fails to account for

cards.front: What does the reading say western scholars over-focus on regarding Christianity?
cards.back: Its movement into the “global south”

cards.front: What do western scholars, Weber among them, get wrong about Confucianism?
cards.back: They treat it as far more prevalent than surveys show — very few in East Asia or the diaspora self-identify as Confucian

cards.front: Why might someone identify as Buddhist or Confucian yet deny being religious?
cards.back: Because they do not consider those traditions to be religions

cards.front: What kind of problem does the reading say underlies people identifying as Buddhist or Confucian while denying they are religious?
cards.back: A language problem — meanings were altered when the terms were translated and imported

cards.front: What does the reading say about the word “religion” in everyday East Asian language?
cards.back: For many, it is still not an everyday concept

cards.front: How does the reading characterise political leadership on what counts as religion?
cards.back: As “confused and confusing”

cards.front: In China, how are Confucianism and Daoism officially classified?
cards.back: Confucianism is not a religion; Daoism is

cards.front: How does the reading describe modern atheism as a confounding factor?
cards.back: As a secularist ideology — a modern phenomenon

cards.front: What does the reading claim about atheism rates in East Asia?
cards.back: By some measures, East Asian societies have the highest proportions of people claiming to be atheists

cards.meaning: Robert Bellah's 1985 concept for Americans who mix and choose their own religion

cards.front: Who introduced Sheilaism, where, and when?
cards.back: Robert Bellah, in America, in 1985

cards.front: Why is Sheilaism relevant to the Global East?
cards.back: The reading argues it can be applied to East Asia in some senses

cards.front: Which related phenomena does the reading say also appear in East Asia?
cards.back: New Age spiritualism, being “spiritual but not religious”, and religious “nones”

cards.front: What was the course of secularization in China?
cards.back: A state-engineered programme — but religiousness has been rising since the 1970s

cards.front: Does the Chinese pattern of secularization hold across the region?
cards.back: No — not all countries follow it

cards.front: What did the first westerners to study Korea observe?
cards.back: That Koreans called on supernatural powers for supernatural reasons

cards.front: Which three traditions have been prominent in Korea since early history?
cards.back: Buddhism, Confucianism, and Shamanism

cards.front: What effect has modernization had on demand for religion in Korea?
cards.back: None — it has not affected it

cards.front: What proportion of Koreans have a religious affiliation, and what is true of the rest?
cards.back: About 50% — and many of those claiming not to be religious still engaged in religious activities

cards.front: How does the reading describe the Korean approach to religion?
cards.back: Instrumentalist — like choosing the best tool for a given job

cards.front: What is the gap between Korean religious groups and Korean practice?
cards.back: Groups sometimes claim exclusivity, but people do not always practise it that way

cards.front: How was Buddhism received when it arrived in Korea?
cards.back: It caused a stir, but was eventually accepted

cards.front: Why did Joseon-dynasty elites adopt Confucianism as the central state ideology?
cards.back: They wanted to be closer to Chinese political thought

cards.front: When did Christianity arrive in Korea, and how was it first received?
cards.back: In the 1700s — as heretical and dangerous, and it was persecuted

cards.front: What is Korea's standing in Christianity in Asia today?
cards.back: The second most Christian country in Asia, and the second largest producer of Christian missionaries

cards.front: Why did Christianity appeal to the lower classes in Korea?
cards.back: Its egalitarian doctrine, against a backdrop of corruption and ineffectualness

cards.front: What helped Christianity gain traction after Japan annexed Korea?
cards.back: Support from the U.S. Army Military Government, and President Rhee Syngman, who vowed to rule South Korea as a Christian nation

cards.front: What do some scholars claim about the antiquity of Korean shamanism?
cards.back: That it goes back to prehistoric times, when Korea was ruled by shaman-kings who were both political and religious leaders

cards.front: What displaced Korean shamanism?
cards.back: Buddhism and Confucianism

cards.front: How long has shamanism been attacked by Korean elites, and with what result?
cards.back: For the last 600 years — yet it has never come close to extinction

cards.front: How is Korean shamanism regarded today?
cards.back: As superstitious and irrational

cards.front: On what axiom does North Korea ban religion?
cards.back: The communist axiom that religion is the opium of the masses

cards.front: What is known about the Buddhist temples and Christian churches in North Korea?
cards.back: Little — information is very hard to get; those familiar think what is practised illustrates state propaganda of religious freedom

cards.meaning: North Korea's unquestioned belief in the superiority of its system and the leadership of the Kim family — standing in place of religion

cards.front: How is South Korea described religiously today?
cards.back: As a multi-religious society

cards.front: Which religion is named as having made sizeable gains in South Korea?
cards.back: Islam

cards.front: Who founded Confucianism, and roughly when and where?
cards.back: Confucius — around 500 BCE, in China

cards.front: On the lecture's account, what role did Confucianism play across East Asian societies?
cards.back: The foundation of their development — the ethical construct that guided them

cards.front: What is Confucianism's central focus?
cards.back: Ethics — what it means to be a good person

cards.front: What attitude to the past does Confucianism hold?
cards.back: Veneration of it

cards.front: How does Confucianism relate individual conduct to society?
cards.back: Conduct is tied to the social order: no one exists as an individual apart from society, so the question is how to be good in relation to it

cards.meaning: children respecting their parents, caring for them, and making sure they are at ease — a core Confucian value

cards.front: What happened when other religions mixed with Confucianism?
cards.back: They became new religions of their own, or a part of Confucianism

cards.front: To whom is Daoism attributed, and roughly when and where?
cards.back: Laozi — 6th century BCE, in China

cards.meaning: “old master” — the figure Daoism is attributed to

cards.front: What is uncertain about Laozi?
cards.back: Whether he was a real person

cards.front: What stance toward worldly affairs does Daoism teach?
cards.back: Passive withdrawal from them

cards.front: Instead of ambition, what does Daoism tell a person to do?
cards.back: Observe nature and copy how it acts — flowing, not rushing — staying in tune with it

cards.front: What quest is Daoism often associated with?
cards.back: Long life, immortality, and overcoming physical limitations

cards.front: According to the lecture, where did many Daoist practices come from?
cards.back: Buddhism

cards.front: What is Shinto?
cards.back: The indigenous religion of Japan

cards.text: Shinto has no {{c1::founder}}, no {{c2::founding date}}, and no {{c3::major sacred text}}

cards.meaning: in Shinto, a spiritual, life-giving force that may inhabit natural phenomena

cards.front: What practical attitude follows from belief in kami?
cards.back: Not harming or annoying the spirits

cards.front: Who founded Buddhism, and roughly when?
cards.back: Siddhārtha Gautama — the 6th or 5th century BCE

cards.front: What status did Buddhism hold in many East Asian countries?
cards.back: State religion

cards.text: Buddhism has a concept of {{c1::heaven and hell}}, of {{c2::saints to worship}}, and of beings {{c3::somewhat like angels}}

cards.front: How many buddhas are there, and which one does the course mean by “the Buddha”?
cards.back: More than one — the course means the historical Buddha

cards.front: What is paradoxical about the historical Buddha's status in Buddhism?
cards.back: He is not considered a god, yet he is one of the objects of worship

cards.front: What institutional system does Buddhism have?
cards.back: Monasticism

cards.front: What do the salvation-oriented Buddhist sects hold?
cards.back: That the world is so corrupt the only way to be saved is for the Buddha to take you to paradise

cards.front: What idea is Buddhism said to have introduced?
cards.back: Funerary rites

cards.front: Which of the major East Asian traditions does the lecture call inclusive rather than exclusive?
cards.back: All four — Confucianism, Daoism, Shinto, and Buddhism

cards.front: Where does the word now widely used for “religion” in East Asia come from?
cards.back: A Japanese translation of the European concept

cards.front: What words were used before it for what we call religion, and still are?
cards.back: “Teaching”, “school of”, “way”, “path”

cards.text: East Asian folk religions have no {{c1::founder}}, no {{c2::founding date}}, and no {{c3::doxa}}

cards.front: What follows from folk religions developing organically, without a clear start?
cards.back: There is no clear division between one religious practice and another

cards.front: What do folk religions tend to focus on?
cards.back: The calendar, ritual cycles, and belief in spirits

cards.front: For whom are folk religions often a form of religious expression?
cards.back: Women — female shamanesses, for example

cards.front: How do folk religions relate to the major traditions?
cards.back: They accommodate and fuse with them

cards.front: Who compiled the Analects, and when?
cards.back: Confucius's disciples, after his death

cards.front: In the Analects, what do the “gentleman” and the “petty person” stand for?
cards.back: The gentleman is always good — the model to follow; the petty person shows what not to do

cards.front: Why is the Analects written in short, pithy sayings?
cards.back: It spoke to an almost completely illiterate population, so it was passed on by memory — each idea distilled to its simplest form

cards.front: According to the 10/01 lecture, how do most religions present themselves?
cards.back: As universal and timeless

cards.front: What did Confucius's ethics draw on?
cards.back: Longstanding ideas of morality

cards.front: Which three things make up goodness, for Confucius?
cards.back: Xiao (filial piety), ren (benevolence) and li (ritual)

cards.front: How are Confucian relationships ordered, and what does each side owe?
cards.back: All but one — friend and friend — are hierarchical. The subordinate must be dutiful; the superior must care for them and be kind. In filial piety, the parents are the superiors.

cards.front: Which practice is part of filial piety, and central to Confucianism?
cards.back: Ancestor worship

cards.front: What does the Analects allow a child to do when their parents are in the wrong, and what must follow?
cards.back: Gently remonstrate with them. If they don't take it to heart, stay respectful, don't oppose them, and follow their lead diligently without resentment.

cards.front: What does Confucius say to do if your parents commit a crime and insist on it?
cards.back: Cover up for them — even by taking the blame yourself

cards.front: How did filial piety apply to a married woman?
cards.back: Her in-laws became like her parents, since a wife moved into her husband's house

cards.meaning: benevolence — the desire to do good; very simply, care for others

cards.text: Ren in the Analects: “Ren is {{c1::to love people}}”; “When in public, comport yourself as if {{c2::you were receiving an important guest}}”; “Do not impose upon others {{c3::what you yourself do not desire}}”

cards.meaning: ritual — doing everything according to the proper rites

cards.front: How far does li, Confucian ritual, reach?
cards.back: From grand state ceremonies to the proper way to fasten one's lapel

cards.front: Where do the rites of li come from, and what idea lies behind that?
cards.back: From older societies, especially the Zhou dynasty — the idea that old things are good

cards.text: Confucius's ethics held that society should be ruled by {{c1::a meritocracy of educated men}}; that all people have {{c2::the capacity for self-cultivation}}; and that society is {{c3::fundamentally unequal}}, bound by {{c4::reciprocal relationships}}
cards.extra: In those relationships, superiors are to be benevolent and subordinates are to obey.

cards.text: The case that Confucianism is not a religion: Confucius is {{c1::not a god or a divine force}}; you needn't {{c2::pray, go to a temple, or read a specific book}}; you needn't {{c3::worship anything or believe Confucius was a god}}; and you can {{c4::practise it as a philosophy}}
cards.extra: From a western perspective this “no” is the most common answer.

cards.front: What caveat weakens “Confucius is not a god” as a reason Confucianism isn't a religion?
cards.back: In East Asia there is no strict line between natural and supernatural, as there is in the West

cards.text: The case that Confucianism is a religion: after Confucius died, {{c1::more religious aspects were added}}; there are {{c2::temples to Confucius, with animal sacrifices and rituals}}; some people {{c3::pray to Confucius}}; and it {{c4::asks you to follow principles to achieve goodness}}, as a religion does

cards.front: What did later temples to Confucius borrow from Buddhism?
cards.back: Ideas such as statues

cards.front: Who was Mengzi, and when did he live?
cards.back: A Confucian philosopher of the 4th century BCE

cards.front: What was Mengzi's relationship to Kongzi (Confucius)?
cards.back: He never met him, but tried to practise and teach Kongzi's Way

cards.front: How is Mengzi ranked in China?
cards.back: Second only to Kongzi in importance

cards.front: What is the Mengzi, and where does the name “Mencius” come from?
cards.back: The collection of Mengzi's sayings; “Mencius” is the Jesuits' Latinisation

cards.front: How is the Mengzi divided?
cards.back: Into 7 books, each with an A and a B part, each divided again into short “chapters” — hence references like 2A6

cards.front: Whose teachings did Mengzi treat as the intellectual opponents of the Way?
cards.back: Yang Zhu's and Mozi's

cards.front: What did Mozi advocate?
cards.back: Universal consequentialism: judging every action only by its consequences for the benefit of all, with everyone's benefit counting equally — hence Mohist “impartial caring”

cards.front: What does Yang Zhu seem to have taught, and how did Mengzi see him?
cards.back: That excessive sacrifice for others goes against human nature. Mengzi saw him as egotistical.

cards.front: Where did Mengzi agree with Yang Zhu, and where did he part ways?
cards.back: He agreed that humans have a nature they should follow, but argued that it contains virtuous inclinations — so ethical cultivation is tending that nature

cards.front: How did Mengzi think people can discover their moral inclinations?
cards.back: Through thought experiments

cards.front: What did Mengzi say destroys the goodness of human nature?
cards.back: A bad environment, and failure to cultivate oneself — the nature is good, but people are not necessarily good

cards.front: What did Mengzi see as a prerequisite for developing a good nature?
cards.back: Basic needs, such as food, being met

cards.front: What does advanced ethical cultivation require, for Mengzi?
cards.back: A teacher

cards.front: How did Mengzi disagree with the Mohists about love?
cards.back: They said love for all should be equally great; he said love for family, kin and those closer must be greater

cards.front: What did Mengzi say of basing one's actions on benefit or profit?
cards.back: That it is self-defeating

cards.front: In Mengzi's Book One, what does he tell a king who wants profit?
cards.back: That he should seek benevolence and righteousness instead

cards.front: What is Mengzi's point in the parable of the soldiers who ran fifty paces?
cards.back: Those who ran fifty paces, laughing at those who ran a hundred, had fled the battle just the same — said to a king who thought he governed well

cards.front: What did a king's pity for an ox being led to sacrifice show, according to Mengzi?
cards.back: That he has compassion

cards.front: Why did Mengzi compare that king to someone who can lift 500 lbs but not a feather?
cards.back: He showed kindness to the ox but not to his people — not because he can't, but because he won't

cards.front: What did Mengzi compare a king's wish to dominate by military force to?
cards.back: Climbing a tree to find a fish

cards.front: What would benevolent government bring a king, according to Mengzi?
cards.back: Everyone would want to come to his markets, fields and roads

cards.front: What does Mengzi call failing to give people a livelihood and then punishing them for crime?
cards.back: Trapping them

cards.text: A good livelihood, for Mengzi: “In good years, one is {{c1::always full}}. In years of famine, one {{c2::escapes death}}” — and one can {{c3::serve one's father and mother, and nurture one's wife and children}}

cards.front: How did Mengzi answer a king who excused himself as fond of wealth, and then as fond of sex?
cards.back: If the ruler lets the common folk have the same — wealth, and the same privileges — that is in line with the Way

cards.text: Mengzi on the execution of King Zhou: one who violates benevolence is {{c1::a thief}}; one who violates righteousness is {{c2::a mutilator}}; such a person is {{c3::a mere fellow}} — “I have heard of the execution of the fellow Zhou, but not of the killing of one's ruler”
cards.extra: The point: a ruler who doesn't act properly is no longer a legitimate ruler.

cards.front: In Mengzi 2A6, what follows if a ruler extends people's natural feeling for others into how he governs?
cards.back: He brings order to the whole world

cards.text: Mengzi's four sprouts (2A6): compassion is the sprout of {{c1::benevolence}}; disdain is the sprout of {{c2::righteousness}}; deference is the sprout of {{c3::propriety}}; approval and disapproval is the sprout of {{c4::wisdom}}
cards.extra: Your notes list three; the second, disdain (shame at wrongdoing), is from the text.

cards.front: According to Mengzi 2A6, what follows if one “fills out” the four sprouts — and if one doesn't?
cards.back: Filled out, they are enough to care for all within the four seas; neglected, one can't even serve one's parents

cards.front: In Mengzi 6A1, what did Gaozi claim, and how did Mengzi answer?
cards.back: Gaozi: human nature has to be moulded into righteousness, as willow is made into bowls. Mengzi: then people must be violated to be made good — which makes benevolence and righteousness a misfortune.

cards.front: What is Gaozi's water analogy for human nature (Mengzi 6A2)?
cards.back: Human nature is like water, which flows out of whatever opening it's given — so it is neutral, neither good nor bad

cards.front: How did Mengzi turn Gaozi's water analogy around?
cards.back: Water naturally flows downward. It can be dammed or splashed upward, but that goes against its nature — so human nature is good.

cards.front: In Mengzi 6A4, what did Gaozi claim about benevolence and righteousness?
cards.back: That benevolence is internal and righteousness external — Mengzi disagreed

cards.front: In Mengzi 6A6, how did Mengzi answer Gaozi's claim that human nature is neither good nor bad?
cards.back: All humans have the potential to be good

cards.front: When did Xunzi live, relative to China's unification?
cards.back: He was one of the last exponents of Confucian thought before unification in 221 BCE

cards.front: In what form has Xunzi's thought come down?
cards.back: Essays

cards.front: How did Xunzi treat Confucianism's critics?
cards.back: He defended Confucianism against them, but learned from them and took in their insights — Zhuangzi's above all, though their views differed a great deal

cards.front: Which threat from within Confucianism did Xunzi see in Mengzi?
cards.back: The idea that human nature is good, which he thought did away with the need for ritual to guide behaviour

cards.front: What did Xunzi mean by saying human nature is bad?
cards.back: Not that people delight in evil, but that they have no inborn guide to right conduct — so they need the external guide of ritual

cards.front: Where does Xunzi agree with Mengzi about goodness, and where does he differ?
cards.back: Everyone has the potential for it — but for Xunzi, reaching it is a very hard and arduous process

cards.front: According to Xunzi (ch. 23), what are people born with?
cards.back: A desire for profit, other desires, and feelings of hate and dislike — and following them is bad

cards.front: Where does following human nature lead, for Xunzi?
cards.back: To strife in society, and eventually violence

cards.front: What does Xunzi say people need in order to reach righteousness?
cards.back: The transforming influence of teachers and models, and the guidance of ritual and righteousness — ritual no one knows from birth

cards.front: What is Xunzi's image of the crooked wood?
cards.back: Crooked wood must await steaming and straightening on the shaping frame; only then does it become straight. Mengzi had objected that shaping people, like turning willow into bowls, violates their nature.

cards.front: Why did the ancients establish ritual, according to Xunzi?
cards.back: To be a good influence on the common people

cards.front: How does Xunzi disagree with Mengzi about learning?
cards.back: For Mengzi, learning brings out people's inherent good; for Xunzi, ritual and righteousness come from effort

cards.front: How does Xunzi tell what comes from inborn nature?
cards.back: Desires come from it: they respond to stimulation with no delay between perception and reaction. So whatever has a delay is not from innate nature.

cards.front: Why does Xunzi say people's wish to be good shows their nature is bad?
cards.back: People desire what they lack

cards.front: What does Xunzi ask of Mengzi's view of ritual?
cards.back: If human nature is good, why would ritual be needed at all? Mengzi would say ritual brings an already-good nature into line with Heaven.

cards.front: What did Mengzi add to Confucianism about authority?
cards.back: That you don't always have to follow it

cards.front: How were Mengzi's ideas received?
cards.back: They were hugely popular, and many of his statements became common sayings

cards.front: What is Mengzi's well analogy meant to show?
cards.back: Everyone has a heart sensitive to others' suffering: anyone who saw a baby about to fall into a well would be alarmed — not to impress the parents or win a good name

cards.front: What does Mengzi say of someone who wouldn't be alarmed by the baby at the well?
cards.back: That they are not a human being — the feeling is that fundamental

cards.front: How did the ancient kings' compassion show itself, for Mengzi?
cards.back: In compassionate policies

cards.front: How do Mengzi's priorities among xiao, li and ren differ from Kongzi's?
cards.back: Kongzi might put xiao and li above ren — not turning in one's parents. Mengzi weighs them differently: see his answer on the killing of King Zhou, and his hint to King Xuan of Qi that a bad government should be removed.

cards.front: What did Xunzi say about the sacrifice for rain?
cards.back: It has no special mechanism — performing it has no effect on the rain

cards.front: If the rain sacrifice does nothing, why does Xunzi say we perform such rites?
cards.back: To give things proper form — though common people take them as contact with spirits. Practised society-wide, they make individuals and society good.

cards.front: Why does Xunzi's view of ritual move Confucianism further from being a “religion” in western eyes?
cards.back: He denies the rites any supernatural effect: they exist for form and moral formation

cards.front: What do Ban Zhao and Song Ruozhao discuss?
cards.back: The Confucian role for women

cards.front: Who founded Neo-Confucianism, and what was it?
cards.back: Zhu Xi, arguably — he drew together the work of earlier Song-dynasty thinkers. It was a revival of Confucianism after a decline.

cards.front: What did Zhu Xi's Neo-Confucianism focus on?
cards.back: The family as the foundational unit, and the practical application of moral principles

cards.text: Kongzi, in one of his only recorded sayings about women: “Women and servants are {{c1::most difficult to nurture}}. If one is close to them, {{c2::they lose their reserve}}, while if one is distant, {{c3::they feel resentful}}.”

cards.front: Until which dynasty was there almost no discussion of what a Confucian ethic for women might be?
cards.back: The Han (206 BCE – 220 CE)

cards.front: Why do some say Confucianism is for men and Daoism for women?
cards.back: Confucianism means actively cultivating oneself and changing things for the better — the masculine yang. Daoism urges passively following the way of nature, in harmony with it — the feminine yin.

cards.front: How did Ban Zhao come to be a court historian?
cards.back: She took up the mantle after her father, Ban Biao, and her brother, Ban Gu, died — and finished the history of the Han they had begun

cards.front: What makes Ban Zhao rare in Chinese literature?
cards.back: She is one of very few women who both wrote and had their writing preserved

cards.front: When did Zhu Xi live, relative to Kongzi?
cards.back: More than 1,500 years later: Zhu Xi lived 1130–1200 CE, Kongzi 551–479 BCE

cards.front: What was the religious climate when Zhu Xi was born, and what did he set out to do?
cards.back: Buddhism was very strong; he wanted to turn the focus back to Confucianism

cards.front: What system did Zhu Xi devise to put Neo-Confucian philosophy into practice?
cards.back: Granaries kept full even in famine — eventually a statewide system. The greatest ren is to care for people.

cards.text: The five relationships Neo-Confucianism made the foundation of a well-ordered society: four hierarchical — {{c1::father–son}}, {{c2::lord–servant}}, {{c3::husband–wife}} and {{c4::older brother–younger brother}} — and one equal, friend–friend
cards.extra: The list goes back to Mengzi (3A4).

cards.front: What became paramount for women under Neo-Confucianism?
cards.back: Female chastity — and with it, footbinding

cards.front: Where did Zhu Xi stand on whether human nature is good?
cards.back: With Mengzi: human nature is principle (li), and so good; evil comes from the material force (qi) that clouds it

cards.front: What was footbinding?
cards.back: Breaking a young girl's feet — at three to five years old — folding the toes under, and binding them tightly so the feet looked extremely small

cards.front: How is footbinding said to have begun?
cards.back: In the 10th century, a ruler of the Southern Tang had his concubine bind her feet to perform a dance

cards.front: How did footbinding spread?
cards.back: By the Song dynasty, prostitutes, dancers and other female entertainers had taken it up; from them it spread to the upper classes

cards.front: Why was footbinding seen as serving chastity?
cards.back: A woman with bound feet couldn't easily leave the house

cards.front: In a society that counted being born a woman a misfortune, how could footbinding turn it to advantage?
cards.back: Bound feet could let a girl marry into the upper classes — a path to social mobility

cards.front: Who, by tradition, wrote the Daodejing, and when did he live?
cards.back: Laozi — an older contemporary of Kongzi

cards.front: What do contemporary scholars say about Laozi and the Daodejing?
cards.back: Laozi is a mythical figure, and the text is a composite work

cards.front: Though the Daodejing was cobbled together from many sources, how does it read?
cards.back: As if it was put together in a fairly short time, possibly by a single editor

cards.front: How many chapters does the Daodejing have, and what are they like?
cards.back: 81 — short passages, some of which rhyme

cards.front: What does the title “Daodejing” mean?
cards.back: “The Classic of Dao and De” — of the Way and Virtue

cards.front: Where does the Daodejing get its title?
cards.back: From the first concept of each of its two books, not from their content: Book I (chapters 1–37) is the Dao half, and Book II (38–81) the De half

cards.front: When was the Daodejing put together, and how does it respond to its times?
cards.back: Near the end of the Warring States period, an age of interstate rivalry. Weary of war and chaos, it longs for security and peace.

cards.front: What does the Daodejing trace wars of expansion and corrupt government to?
cards.back: Greed and ambition — hence its view that desire must be limited if it isn't to cause harm

cards.front: What earlier time does the Daodejing appeal to?
cards.back: A time when goodness was reflexive and instinctive, not thought out

cards.front: What place do human beings have in the Dao?
cards.back: A place, but not an exalted one: they are one kind of thing among others

cards.front: Why do human beings upset the harmony of the Dao, and what does the Daodejing seek to do about it?
cards.back: They can alter the nature of things, so they tend to forsake their natural place. The text seeks to undo this.

cards.front: What kind of text does the introduction call the Daodejing, rather than a presentation of theory?
cards.back: Philosophical therapy

cards.front: How do opposites relate, according to the Daodejing?
cards.back: They harmonise with and offset each other (ch. 2)

cards.text: The Daodejing: revering important people leads to {{c1::strife}}; revering material possessions leads to {{c2::theft}}

cards.front: Where does the Daodejing mention a lord or god, and in what context?
cards.back: Only once, in chapter 4: the Dao is “the image of what was before the Lord himself”

cards.front: Who is the “Enigmatic Female” in the Daodejing?
cards.back: The spirit of the valley — her gate is the root of Heaven and earth (ch. 6)

cards.front: What paradox does the Daodejing see in the sages?
cards.back: They put themselves last, yet come first; having no thought of themselves, they are able to perfect themselves (ch. 7)

cards.text: The Daodejing on where the good lies: “In a residence, the good lies in {{c1::location}}. In hearts, the good lies in {{c1::depth}}. In interactions with others, the good lies in {{c2::benevolence}}. In words, the good lies in {{c2::trustworthiness}}. In government, the good lies in {{c3::orderliness}}. In carrying out one's business, the good lies in {{c3::ability}}. In actions, the good lies in {{c4::timeliness}}. Only by {{c4::avoiding contention}} can one avoid blame.”

cards.front: What does the Daodejing say comes of being haughty about one's prestige and wealth?
cards.back: One brings disaster on oneself (ch. 9)

cards.front: How does the Daodejing want a ruler to lead?
cards.back: Caring for the people and ordering the state, but without lording it over them (ch. 10)

cards.front: What is the point of the Daodejing's clay vessel and room?
cards.back: What's useful is what's absent: we shape clay into a vessel but use its cavity, and doors, walls and windows make a room but we use the space they leave (ch. 11)

cards.front: What does the Daodejing say constant chasing and hunting do to us?
cards.back: They madden our hearts (ch. 12)

cards.front: In the Daodejing, what does revering and caring for your own body show?
cards.back: That you're worthy of being trusted with more responsibility (ch. 13, which says to “revere calamity as you revere your own body”)

cards.front: What does the Daodejing say stillness does to muddy water?
cards.back: Makes it clear — where movement stirs up what was still (ch. 15)

cards.front: What does the Daodejing keep urging a return to?
cards.back: A better, more natural state

cards.front: Which ruler does the Daodejing rank above one who is loved and praised?
cards.back: One who is “but a shadowy presence” — and a loved ruler is better than one who is feared and reviled (ch. 17)

cards.front: What paradox about loss and gain does the Daodejing draw?
cards.back: As more can lead to less, so less can yield more: good comes out of bad circumstances (ch. 22)

cards.front: What does the Daodejing repeatedly say comes of abandoning something good?
cards.back: Something good — overthinking, it seems, gets in the way of goodness

cards.front: When, according to the Daodejing, do virtues become noticeable?
cards.back: Only when something has gone wrong — filial piety shows when families are at odds, loyal ministers when the state is in chaos (ch. 18)

cards.front: When the Daodejing's author shifts into the first person, what do they say of themselves and the common folk?
cards.back: That they are at a loss, while the common folk are “bright and brilliant” (ch. 20)

cards.front: What does the Daodejing say bragging and self-aggrandisement lead to?
cards.back: People not liking you (ch. 24)

cards.front: What does the Way model itself on, according to the Daodejing?
cards.back: What is natural. Humans model themselves on Earth, Earth on Heaven, and Heaven on the Way (ch. 25).

cards.front: What does the Daodejing say of those who are truly good at something — and so of sages?
cards.back: They make no mistakes and need no crutches; so sages save people and never abandon anyone (ch. 27)

cards.front: Which line of the Daodejing counsels holding to the feminine?
cards.back: “Know the male but preserve the female” (ch. 28)

cards.front: What does the Daodejing say comes of taking the world by force of arms?
cards.back: It comes back in kind (ch. 30)

cards.front: What is the Daodejing's stance on weapons?
cards.back: All creatures find them repulsive, so one who is on the Way doesn't rely on them — but may use them when there is no choice (ch. 31)

cards.front: What does the Daodejing say of reveling in victory?
cards.back: It is reveling in the slaughter of human beings, and one who delights in that won't achieve his ambitions (ch. 31)

cards.front: What does the Daodejing say about striving for virtue?
cards.back: It isn't how you gain virtue (ch. 38)

cards.front: What does the stability of Heaven and earth show, according to the Daodejing?
cards.back: That they have “attained the One” — so they don't tear themselves apart (ch. 39)

cards.front: What does the Daodejing say about how the Way appears?
cards.back: It may not seem level, or to lead forward, but it is — and only the Way is good at providing and completing (ch. 41)

cards.front: How does everything arise from the Way, according to the Daodejing?
cards.back: The Way produces the One, its representation; the One produces the two, yin and yang; the two produce the three; and the three produce everything in the world (ch. 42)

cards.front: What kind of process is the Daodejing's account of how everything arises from the Way?
cards.back: A natural progression, with no creator or higher power

cards.text: The Daodejing: “Know {{c1::contentment}} and avoid disgrace; know {{c2::when to stop}} and avoid danger; and you will {{c3::long endure}}”

cards.front: Whom is the Daodejing's sage good to, and whom does he trust?
cards.back: The good and the bad alike; the trustworthy and those who aren't, alike (ch. 49)

cards.front: What does the Daodejing say understanding the world and its source allows?
cards.back: Avoiding danger (ch. 52) — the source being the Way, or the One

cards.front: What does the Daodejing call strength?
cards.back: Preserving the weak (ch. 52)

cards.front: What does the Daodejing call possessing wealth in gross abundance while the granaries are empty?
cards.back: Taking pride in robbery (ch. 53)

cards.front: When does the Daodejing say to put things in order?
cards.back: Before they become disordered — preparing is easy while things are going well (ch. 64)

cards.front: What does the Daodejing say of those good at fighting, and of generals?
cards.back: They aren't overly aggressive and don't start fights; generals don't want to make the first move (ch. 68–69)

cards.front: What question does the Daodejing say even sages find difficult?
cards.back: Why Heaven dislikes what it does (ch. 73)

cards.front: What lesson does the Daodejing draw from water's suppleness?
cards.back: The weak overcome the strong: nothing is more supple or weak than water, yet nothing can surpass it or resist its advance (ch. 78)

cards.text: The Daodejing's ideal people {{c1::use no labour-saving tools, ships or carts}}, {{c2::keep track with knots instead of writing}} and {{c3::don't travel}} — yet {{c4::their food is savoury, their clothes fine, their houses comfortable and their lives happy}}

cards.front: What do some scholars think “Laozi” was, if not one man?
cards.back: A name taken by a group of people — some even think a group of women

cards.front: Why do some think a group of women may have taken the name Laozi?
cards.back: Women weren't allowed to be philosophers, and Daoism values qualities Chinese culture held inferior — women among them

cards.front: How does the theory that Laozi was a group fit Daoist thought?
cards.back: It fits the Daoist idea that no one person is above the rest

cards.front: What does “Daoism” literally translate as?
cards.back: “Way-ism” — dao means “way”

cards.front: How does the Daodejing's style differ from the Analects'?
cards.back: The Analects is straightforward and conversational; the Daodejing is cryptic, poetic and opaque

cards.front: Why is the Daodejing full of repeated sounds?
cards.back: To break you away from everyday thinking

cards.front: Besides its key concepts, what two things does Daoism distrust?
cards.back: Words — it is wary of language as an expression of the Truth, or the Way — and society. Both can lead people astray.

cards.front: If words fail to express the Way, what does Daoism turn to?
cards.back: The yin and the yang

cards.text: Daoism's key concepts: {{c1::the Way}}, {{c2::yin-yang}}, {{c3::water}} and {{c4::balance}}

cards.front: What is the Way, in Daoism?
cards.back: A cosmic force, or the natural order — the ideal state and the root of all things. Human beings should live in harmony with it.

cards.text: What the yin-yang picture teaches: {{c1::all things are equal}}; {{c2::life is constant flux}}; {{c3::pushing to one extreme brings its opposite}}; {{c4::each thing holds the seed of its opposite}}; and {{c5::evil is imbalance, not the dark half}}

cards.front: What does the equal size of the yin-yang's halves teach?
cards.back: That things are equal — neither half is higher, and both are needed to make an integrated whole, even things you might not prefer in this life

cards.front: What does it mean that each half of the yin-yang is moving into the other?
cards.back: Nothing is static: life is a constant flux, a balancing out of two opposites

cards.front: What does the yin-yang teach where each side grows thickest, just as it turns into the other?
cards.back: Push too far to one extreme and you get its opposite

cards.front: What does the dot of the other colour in each half of the yin-yang teach?
cards.back: The seeds of each thing's opposite exist within it

cards.front: If the yin-yang's white and dark halves aren't good and evil, what is true evil in Daoism?
cards.back: The imbalance of the two sides

cards.meaning: “non-action” — avoiding purposeful action; one of Daoism's main concepts, stressed again and again in the Daodejing

cards.text: The lecture's illustration of wuwei, from the Daodejing: “Everyone knows that when the beautiful strives to be beautiful, {{c1::it is repulsive}}. Everyone knows that when good strives to be good, {{c2::it is no good}}.”
cards.extra: Chapter 2. Self-conscious striving to excel at something good is counterproductive.

cards.front: Why does Daoism counsel against purposeful action?
cards.back: Trying to attain something leads to grief — harm comes from pushing too hard toward a goal. We naturally, unconsciously strive for a middle path, and avoiding purposeful action is how to reach it.

cards.front: How, in Daoism, do you work out what to do?
cards.back: Passively emulate the natural order: first observe nature and your surroundings; once you've worked out their natural order, act in harmony with it, avoiding extremes

cards.front: Why is water the Daodejing's example of the highest good, and a key Daoist symbol?
cards.back: Water benefits everything without causing harm or strife, and doesn't avoid what people think inferior — it shows how to live in accordance with the Way (ch. 8)

cards.front: Where do Daoism and Confucianism each find the way to harmony and peace?
cards.back: Daoism: in the individual's place within the cosmos, the natural order. Confucianism: in appropriate human relationships within the social order — for it, the only order worth following.

cards.front: Why does Daoism say society's rules should not always be followed?
cards.back: Society often puts the individual in opposition to the natural order

cards.front: What does Confucianism say people must do, and how should it be rewarded?
cards.back: Actively cultivate themselves — and be rewarded with important positions in government

cards.front: Why does Daoism reject the Confucian call to self-cultivation?
cards.back: Actively pursuing a goal brings about its opposite: rewarding self-cultivation makes people fight among themselves for the rewards, ending in chaos, strife and ignorance

cards.front: What else is Siddhārtha Gautama called, and what was he before he became a monk?
cards.back: The historical Buddha, or Shakyamuni — a prince who renounced his position to become a monk

cards.front: Where did Buddhism begin, and when did it reach China?
cards.back: In India. It reached China during the Han dynasty, around the 2nd century CE, and spread from there throughout East Asia.

cards.front: What are the two main branches of Buddhism?
cards.back: Theravāda and Mahāyāna

cards.front: What distinguishes Theravāda Buddhism, and where is it more popular?
cards.back: It most closely reflects the original Buddhism Siddhārtha Gautama taught. It's more popular in Southeast Asia.

cards.front: What distinguishes Mahāyāna Buddhism, and where is it more popular?
cards.back: It's the most popular form of Buddhism in the world today, and it brings many beings into the tradition: monks, saints, incarnations of the Buddha. It's more popular in East Asia.

cards.meaning: a winged messenger of the Buddha, in Mahāyāna Buddhism
one who was a human being and, instead of achieving nirvana, helps others reach enlightenment — in Mahāyāna Buddhism
a holy monk who has achieved enlightenment — a model for his community, prayed to after death for guidance toward enlightenment

cards.front: Where does the professor place Vajrayāna Buddhism, which is sometimes called a third branch?
cards.back: Within Mahāyāna Buddhism

cards.text: The beliefs all branches of Buddhism share: {{c1::reincarnation (samsara)}}, {{c2::karma}}, {{c3::nirvana}}, {{c4::the Four Noble Truths}} and {{c5::the Eightfold Path}}

cards.meaning: reincarnation: after death, something like one's soul passes into another body
“action”: how one's past life's actions shape one's reincarnation
getting out of the cycle of reincarnation — the goal, since reincarnation isn't considered a good thing

cards.text: The Four Noble Truths: {{c1::life is suffering}}; {{c2::the origin of suffering is desire}}; {{c3::the cessation of suffering is achievable}}; {{c4::the Eightfold Path is the way to end suffering}}

The Eightfold Path: right {{c1::view}}, right {{c2::intention}}, right {{c3::speech}}, right {{c4::action}}, right {{c5::livelihood}}, right {{c6::effort}}, right {{c7::mindfulness}} and right {{c8::concentration}}
cards.extra: Right intention is also translated right thought. Right concentration is meditation.

cards.front: How do the branches of Buddhism differ over enlightenment?
cards.back: Each has its own idea of what you should do to achieve it

cards.front: What did Buddhism bring to cultures that, as far as we know, didn't have it before?
cards.back: Ideas of heaven and hell

cards.front: How does heaven in Buddhism differ from Heaven in Confucianism?
cards.back: In Buddhism, heaven is a paradise, and hell exists too. In Confucianism, Heaven is the cosmic order.

cards.front: How do heaven and hell relate to reincarnation in Buddhism?
cards.back: Through reincarnation you can move up and down between the levels, Earth included — but once in heaven or hell, it's harder to move
